title: Virtuele Brigade
problem: I joined a VR training sim project that had been in the works for years, and my job was to add multiplayer and VR support to it, quite a task.
approach: A lot of careful surgery later, instructors could run shared scenarios together in VR, desktop, in editor, it all works. I was responsible for development, lot's of refactoring of code architecture and for the UX flow of the whole application. It gets wheeled out at events and will replace the previous software package used in training new KMar agents, which I’m pretty proud of.
outcome: Multiplayer VR, retrofitted into a long running project
lesson: Adding tech to a system that already exists is often harder than starting from scratch. Before i implement a feature i should ask: 'will this even be maintained?'

title: Alliander HoloLens suite
problem: Alliander has to drop transformers into neighbourhoods where people are not waiting for an ugly box in view so they complain, but the energy transition has to start somewhere. Paper plans were used to decide on a location, this could be improved upon.
approach: We combined RTK GPS, an Android phone, a HoloLens and a backend together so specialists could literally see the transformerhouse floating in exactly the right spot on the real street, to the centimeter. The sighting can be saved and reviewed, visuals give an immediate idea of the resulting environment. I was responsible for development and for the UX flow of the application.
outcome: Visuals that line up with the world to the cm
lesson: The tech was the easy half. But getting it to fit how an organisation actually works was the real puzzle and eventual downfall of this project, it did not catch on due to impracticallities. If it were up to me i would not choose a Hololens but an iPad instead.

title: Alliander digital twin
problem: Engineers were driving out to the same sites over and over, to check the measurements and sizing of a transformerhouse
approach: I built a web tool that mashes laser scans, 360° photos and equipment models together, so they could walk the site from their desk and try things out before anyone got in a van.
outcome: Site visits you can do from your chair
lesson: Technically it worked great, but the organisation wasn’t quite ready to change how it worked so it never fully landed.

title: ARCam
problem: Niantic wanted to hand event visitors a real photo with their favourite characters from the IP's they work with. Think Pokémon, Monster Hunter beasts, basketball stars, the Niantic mascot. It all had to work first time, on a busy show floor, in a different city every other week.
approach: ARCam, an AR photo installation I built at Wonderment for Niantic. An iPad running the Lightship SDK drops the characters into the scene through a viewfinder that came in a few builds, a sturdy pedestal and 2 portable tripod rigs. Two modes: take a photo with the characters (the main event) or pan around to spot location-based highlights out in the world.
outcome: ARCam activations, 16 cities worldwide, all packed in a suitcase
lesson: Location-based AR is a systems-integration problem most of all: the physical world is your least reliable dependency, so you end up owning everything. The tracking, databases, web, audio, performance, devices, UX, 3D, even the electronics and broken screws. The backend was an attempt I built on a hunch, vibe-coded years before that was a phrase; it fell over on day one and then ran flawlessly, which taught me how much value you can add just by taking the initiative early. And living out of a suitcase across all of these cities taught me what ‘delivering’ really means.

title: Wonderment location XR experiments
problem: We kept circling the same question: what can you actually build when digital content is pinned to a real place, how can we tell stories about the places you visit
approach: A run of location-based experiments: GPS and map-anchored AR prototypes that tie content to real coordinates, poking at how it behaves out in the wild rather than on a tidy desk. I'm especially proud of a concept i developed myself completely which guides a tourist through the landings from operation Market Garden, which shows the allied liberation attempt at my birthplace, a story i really wanted to help tell.
outcome: A bunch of location-anchored AR prototypes
lesson: The real world is messy: GPS drifts, places change and people wander into frame. So designing for that mess up front beats pretending it isn't there.

title: DTT Projects
problem: How do i get started in building interesting project that ship to big clients? That was when i landed an internship at DTT where i quickly learned that this was the right career for me even through the challenges that came up from time to time
approach: I worked across a run of projects here: educational reading games, iOS optimization, a space VR experience, an AR sample & showcase app that shows off what the tech can do.
outcome: A shelf of shipped AR / VR / app projects, a flying start to my experience working in and even leading a team of developers
lesson: Everyone is pretending until they figure it out. My dedication to a project and willingness to try is what landed me these projects and i should lean into that.

title: Lightship Drive
problem: Show off shared, multiplayer AR on a noisy trade-show floor with terrible connection, about the most difficult environment you can imagine for a tech demo.
approach: A multiplayer AR racing game with spectator screens, synced audio and a server holding it all together. People racing little AR cars across a real table together. The track on the table changes every 30 seconds, the cars play a version of tag where the crown can be captured from the leading player.
outcome: AR races on a show floor (and they actually worked)
lesson: Build assuming things will fail, because on a show floor they absolutely will. In this case the server SDK was brand new and cut off sessions after some 10 minutes, not seeing a fix i introduced a 'you won! give the phone to the next visitor' popup when the server decided to close.

title: Zwijsen AR books
problem: Zwijsen approached me with an interesting assignment. There was a new edition of a classic book coming out, they wanted to spotlight this release with a companion app that would bring the book to life.
approach: I designed, built and shipped the AR app, from concepting and UX to the technical details of store page submissions. The release was so succesful that we ended up doing 6 more book releases and a series of audiobook apps tied to printed books via QR codes.
outcome: The apps ended up on tens of thousands of phones
lesson: Owning something end to end teaches you the whole lifecycle and that the last 10% (support, store reviews, weird customer feedback) is most of the work.

title: Popcore games
problem: Hyper-casual games live and die by speed: it should ship fast, perform well, and kill it if it flops, then repeat the cycle. Question is: can we make the next hit game?
approach: I built new games but also additions to existing titles, multiplayer features and tools for level and game designers, including for big titles like Parking Jam and Pull the Pin.
outcome: Lots of tiny games, shipped fast
lesson: Shipping fast and iterating beats elegant code. The market really doesn’t care how pretty your architecture is.

title: Philips medical XR & AI
problem: Could emerging XR and AI actually be useful in a clinical setting, or were we just making cool demos and calling it research?
approach: I worked on a few answers: we improved VR equipment demos, did Vision Pro experiments, and worked on a synthetic-data project that generated fake humans in Unreal to train heartbeat-detection from plain video.
outcome: Research that matters and ended up being used in hospitals
lesson: Research is as much about finding out what you shouldn’t build as what you should. “This isn’t worth it” that's still a valueable outcome, better to find that out early than late.

title: Amsterdam AI guides
problem: I wanted to know if an AI tour guide could feel like a person instead of a chatbot. Fictional Amsterdam locals you could actually talk to.
approach: A prototype stitching together speech-to-text, an LLM, text-to-speech and facial animation into characters you hold an conversation with in AR.
outcome: AI locals you can actually chat with in the city
lesson: Just because you can automate the human out of something doesn’t mean you should. This prototype was functional and i made tutorials, documentation, everything. Still it wasn't doing what we hoped it did and ended up on the shelf.

title: Custom AR framework
problem: Back before AR Foundation existed, ARKit and ARCore were two separate worlds, and cross-platform AR meant maintaining two codebases. Could we bridge this divide?
approach: For my graduation I built a framework that unified both behind one API and even ran cloud anchors so the experience could be shared between an Android and iPhone
outcome: Two AR platforms working together in one tidy API. The lesson was mostly a technical one, how to set up this project so it will be maintainable and used in the future.
lesson: Building the tool underneath often creates more value than solving the one problem in front of you.

title: Kastwezens
problem: Festivals are full of interactive experiences, but most people are still consuming instead of creating. We wondered if we could build something that blurred that line. What if a simple drawing on paper could become part of the world around you?
approach: We spent a weekend in the woods building a network of colourful cabinets suspended between the trees. Visitors draw a butterfly, scan it, and within seconds it appears as a living digital creature projected onto the forest, fluttering from cabinet to cabinet. Under the hood it's a mix of Arduino, Unity, webcams, computer vision and projection mapping, but the goal was never to show off the technology. The goal was to create that split second where someone realizes, “Wait... that's my butterfly.”
outcome: Draw a butterfly, watch it fly.
lesson: This project reminded me that the best interactive installations don't ask people to press a button. They invite people to leave something of themselves behind. Nobody talks about the webcam, the UV mapping or the projection setup afterwards. They talk about the butterfly they made and watched disappear into the trees. That's exactly the kind of technology I want to build.

title: Land of the Midnight Sun
problem: How do you tell an emotional story without using a single line of dialogue? That became the central challenge of this student project. We wanted players to feel connected to the world through exploration, atmosphere and gameplay alone.
approach: I led a multidisciplinary team in building a third-person adventure where players guide a young girl through the harsh northern wilderness with the help of an owl companion. Alongside leading the project, I focused on building systems that could grow with the game, integrating audio through FMOD, improving performance and creating animation workflows that helped bring the world to life.
outcome: A dialogue-free adventure inspired by Sami mythology.
lesson: This was the first project that showed me software isn't just about writing good code. Every technical decision influences the experience someone has on screen. Winning first place throughout the competition was rewarding, but the bigger takeaway was learning how to align programmers, artists and designers around a single creative vision.

title: Sol.AR
problem: Space is difficult to grasp because everything about it is unimaginably large. A textbook can tell you Saturn has rings, but it's hard to appreciate them until you're standing inside them. I wanted to build something that made space feel less like information and more like a place you could explore.
approach: Using ARCore, I turned a room into a miniature solar system. You can walk around the planets at scale, inspect them up close and discover interesting facts as you explore. If something catches your attention, you can travel to the surface of that planet or moon to learn more, visit the Mars rovers or even float around the International Space Station. The goal wasn't scientific accuracy down to the millimetre—it was to spark the same sense of curiosity that made me fall in love with space in the first place.
outcome: Bring the solar system into your living room.
lesson: I've always believed the best way to learn is by exploring. AR is uniquely good at turning abstract ideas into physical experiences, and this project showed me that sometimes wonder is a better teacher than information.

title: Amsterdam Underground
problem:
The Municipality of Amsterdam had a VR game that taught players about the hidden world beneath the city's streets. It had been built as a student project and, for its time, it was impressive. But years later it no longer ran on modern hardware, and the request landed on my desk: could you update it for an upcoming event?

Within an hour of opening the project, I knew the answer was no. Not because it was poorly made, but because it had been built to demonstrate an idea, not to evolve. The networking was woven through every gameplay system, dependencies were outdated and simply getting the project to compile required upgrading half the stack. This wasn't going to be an update. It had to become a rebuild.
approach:
Before writing a single line of code, I spent two days doing detective work. Every scene, every button and every multiplayer interaction had to answer the same question: does this still deserve to exist? Once the architecture became clear, I rebuilt the networking layer around Photon Fusion 2, migrated the project to standalone Quest headsets and modernised the visual experience with improved rendering, shaders, haptics and audio.

I deliberately ignored problems that weren't blocking the project. The gameplay wasn't perfect and the balance could have been improved, but those weren't the reasons the game had stopped working. My goal wasn't to create a different game. It was to give the existing one another decade of life.
outcome: Bringing a legacy multiplayer VR experience back to life.
lesson: Legacy projects reward judgement more than programming. Every hour spent polishing the wrong thing is an hour you never get back. This project reminded me that good engineering isn't fixing everything you find—it's recognising what matters, what can wait and having the confidence to leave the rest alone.
